h1_clean: I Have Been Summoned Through The Surrogate's Court. Do I Have To Go, And Do I Need A Lawyer?
meta_desc: A Surrogate's Court citation means a New York estate proceeding affects your rights. What it is, what happens if you ignore it, and when you need counsel.
direct_answer: What you received is almost certainly a citation — the Surrogate's Court's version of a summons. It does not mean you are in trouble. It means a proceeding, often the probate of a will or the appointment of an estate administrator, could affect your legal rights, and the court is giving you a chance to be heard. You are not required to show up, but if you stay silent, the court will treat you as having no objection and the case will proceed without you.

sections.h2: What A Surrogate's Court Citation Actually Means
sections.html:
New York requires that certain people get formal notice before an estate proceeding moves forward — typically the closest living relatives, people named in a will, and anyone whose share would change based on what the court does. If you received a citation, you are on that list.

The citation names a return date. Despite how it sounds, the return date is usually not a trial or a hearing where anyone testifies. It is a calendar date. It is the deadline for you to tell the court, in effect, whether you consent, want more information, or intend to object to what is being requested.

Read the citation carefully: it states what relief is being sought — admitting a will to probate, appointing an administrator, approving an accounting — and that tells you exactly what is at stake for you.

Citations are routine. Surrogate's Courts across New York — including the busy Nassau and Suffolk County courts on Long Island — issue them in nearly every estate proceeding, because the law requires notice before anyone's rights are affected. Receiving one means you matter to the case. Nothing more, and nothing less.

sections.h2: What Happens If You Ignore It
sections.html:
Ignoring a citation does not stop anything. It is the opposite: your silence is treated as consent. If you fail to appear by the return date, the court can grant the relief requested — admit the will, appoint the fiduciary, approve the accounting — and you will generally be bound by that outcome.

That can matter enormously. If the will being offered cuts you out and you might have grounds to challenge it, doing nothing forfeits the opportunity. If an accounting shows an executor paid themselves questionable fees, failing to object waives your complaint. Defaults in Surrogate's Court are difficult to undo later.

If you genuinely have no objection — you have read the papers, you understand them, and the outcome seems right — you may not need to do anything, or you can sign a waiver and consent to speed things along. Just make that choice deliberately, not by letting a deadline pass unread.

You are allowed to appear for yourself, and an appearance can often be made by mail or by an attorney — showing up in person is frequently unnecessary. Whether you need counsel depends on the stakes:

  • You likely need a lawyer if the will disinherits you or treats you unexpectedly, if you suspect undue influence or incapacity, if significant money or real estate is involved, or if you are being asked to approve an accounting you do not fully understand.
  • A lawyer can appear for you, preserve your deadlines, request the examinations New York allows before deciding whether to file objections, and negotiate on your behalf.
  • If you are a business entity that was cited, New York generally requires you to appear through an attorney.

At a minimum, have someone review the papers before the return date. A short consultation before the deadline preserves options; a missed deadline eliminates them.

takeaways: A citation is notice that an estate proceeding could affect your rights — not an accusation.
The return date is a deadline to respond, not usually a hearing with testimony.
If you do nothing, the court treats your silence as consent and the case proceeds without you.
An attorney can appear for you, often without you ever going to court.
Get the papers reviewed before the return date — options disappear once it passes.
faq_short: A Surrogate's Court citation is New York's formal notice that an estate proceeding — often probate of a will — may affect your rights. You are not required to attend, but if you fail to appear by the return date, the court treats you as consenting and can grant the relief requested. If the outcome affects your inheritance or raises concerns, have a lawyer review it before the deadline.
